sections.0.body.0.t: A secret in the cloud is anything that grants access: an API key, a database password, a service token, a private certificate. The critical point is not storing the value, it is controlling who can read it, at what moment, and with what trail.

sections.0.body.1.t: Three practices repeat in any mature architecture: the secret lives in a vault (Vault, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store), the application reads it at run time (not at build time), and its lifetime is short. A credential valid for a year stays useful to an attacker for up to 365 days after a leak, if nobody revokes it, and that is where the real risk lives.

sections.1.body.0.t: The same plot shows up every week: someone commits an AWS Access Key to a public repository or a chat. Miner bots sweep GitHub in minutes, find the key, check whether it still works and start mining crypto on the victim's reserved instances. The bill arrives before the alert.

sections.1.body.1.t: The detail that kills: the key was in an environment variable, so the team thought they had not 'committed a secret'. But the .env.example with a placeholder, the screenshot of the cloud console, the CI log with the value printed... each of these leaks. Scanning for 'AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID' in the repository before merge is basic hygiene that almost nobody does.

sections.2.body.0.t: The old way is static: create an IAM user for the application, generate Access Key + Secret, paste into .env and run. The secret stays valid until someone revokes it, and each new deploy multiplies who holds a copy.

sections.2.body.1.t: The modern way is workload identity. On AWS it is called IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts), on GCP it is Workload Identity, on Azure it is Workload Identity Federation. The idea is the same: the cluster (EKS, GKE, AKS) hands a short-lived token to the pod, and the cloud exchanges that token for temporary credentials via STS/OIDC. There is no static secret to leak.

sections.2.code.0.code.t:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-frontend
  namespace: prod
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/app-frontend-prod

sections.2.code.1.code.t:
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA...         # NEVER do this
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalr...       # never in a versioned file

sections.3.body.0.t: When the workload cannot assume a federated identity (common in older services or third-party SaaS), the alternative is to fetch the secret from the vault at application startup, mount it in memory and never persist it to disk.

sections.3.body.1.t: The difference between fetching at runtime and copying at build is the difference between the secret existing in a Docker image (which someone can open) and existing only on the heap of the running process. The second scenario can still leak via log or dump, but it is orders of magnitude harder.

sections.3.heading.t: Reading from the vault at runtime

sections.4.body.0.t: Rotation is the exercise of replacing a secret before it expires on its own or before someone compromises it. Modern vaults treat this as a first-class citizen: Secrets Manager has automatic rotation via Lambda, Vault has dynamic secrets that expire in minutes, and Parameter Store holds values but does not rotate by itself (use Secrets Manager for that).

sections.4.body.1.t: The practical rule: if you cannot rotate the key without downtime, you cannot revoke the key under pressure. And under pressure is when revocation needs to happen.

sections.4.heading.t: Rotation: why the 5-year-old key is a risk

sections.5.bullets.0.t: application startup: the vault SDK reads the secrets at boot, exposes them in-memory and fails closed if the vault is down

sections.5.bullets.1.t: CI/CD: pipeline secrets come from the provider's vault, never from the runner's global variables

sections.5.bullets.2.t: database deploy: automatic RDS password rotation via Lambda + Secrets Manager, with no maintenance window

sections.5.bullets.3.t: incident response: central revocation takes down all copies in seconds, and the next startup picks up the new value

sections.5.heading.t: Where it fits in day-to-day work

sections.6.bullets.0.t: centralization: a single panel shows who has which secret and when it was last used

sections.6.bullets.1.t: immediate revocation: remove access in the vault, and all applications lose the secret on the next request

sections.6.bullets.2.t: rotation without downtime: databases, API keys and tokens can be swapped with the application live

sections.7.bullets.0.t: workload identity requires fine-grained configuration (OIDC, trust policy, audience) that is easy to get wrong in new clusters

sections.7.bullets.1.t: secrets still leak through logs, dumps or code errors: nothing replaces log scanning with a vault

sections.7.bullets.2.t: cost and latency: reading per request can add hundreds of milliseconds and a few cents per million calls

tagline.t: API keys, database tokens and secrets leave the repository and move to vaults with automatic rotation, short-lived identity and centralized audit logging.
